```{r}
# install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)
```

# Problem 1

The random sample $\{{X}_i, i:1\to n\}$ is drawn from an exponential distribution with pdf $f(x,\theta) = \frac{1}{\theta}\exp\left(-\frac{x}{\theta}\right)$. The following statistics are considered as estimators for $\theta$: $$
T_1 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \quad \mbox{and}\quad T_2 =\Bigg[\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n  X_i^2\Bigg]^{1/2}\,.$$

## a)

Write a function for each of the two estimators.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
T_1 = function(x){mean(x)}

T_2 = function(x){sqrt(0.5*mean(x^2))}
```

## b)

Now write two functions. The first one should compute the bias of a given statistical quantity. The second one should compute the MSE of that statistical quantity. The bias and MSE can be defined as $$Bias = E(\hat T_i) - \theta \quad \text{and} \quad  MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{T_i} - \theta)^2,$$ where $\theta$ is the true value.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
bias = function(x,w){mean(x) - w}

MSE = function(x, w){mean((x-w)^2)}
```

## c)

Draw a random sample and estimate $\theta$ (the mean) using the first estimator. Repeat this procedure to calculate the MSE. Compare this result to the MSE decomposition, i.e. $MSE = Bias^2 + Variance$. Does the decomposition hold?

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
# Parameters
n     = 100   # sample size of Exp(theta)
N_MC  = 1000  # Repetitions of the simulation
theta = 5     # true parameter value
set.seed(123)

# Estimate the mean
T_1_sim = replicate(N_MC, T_1(rexp(n, rate = 1/theta)))

# Compute and compare the MSE formulas
MSE_1 = MSE(T_1_sim, theta)
MSE_2 = bias(T_1_sim, theta)^2 + var(T_1_sim)

list(MSE_1 = MSE_1, MSE_2=MSE_2, Error = abs(MSE_1 - MSE_2))

```

## d)

Simulate biases for $T_1$ and $T_2$. Then plot their empirical densities and indicate their means. Are the estimators biased?

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE, fig.align='center'}
# Added parameter
N_MC_2 = 1000  # Repetitions of the 2nd simulation
set.seed(123)

# Compute the biases 
bias_t1 = replicate(N_MC_2, bias(replicate(N_MC, T_1(rexp(n, rate = 1/theta))), theta))
bias_t2 = replicate(N_MC_2, bias(replicate(N_MC, T_2(rexp(n, rate = 1/theta))), theta))

```

The histograms:

```{r}
# Plot 1
hist(bias_t1, breaks = 'Scott', probability = T, main = 'emp. density of bias_t1')
abline(v = mean(bias_t1), col = 'darkseagreen', lwd = 2)
# Plot 2
hist(bias_t2, breaks = 'Scott', probability = T, main = 'emp. density of bias_t2')
abline(v = mean(bias_t2), col = 'orange1', lwd = 2)
```

## e)

Compute the variance for both estimators as a function of sample size and compare this to the CRLB using a meaningful figure. Add a legend to this figure. Do the estimators reach the CRLB? Can you verify the CRLB theorem? Hints: The CRLB for an exponentially distributed random variable is $CRLB = \frac{\theta^2}{n}$.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE, fig.align='center', fig.width = 10}
# Start with n=3 
n = 3:100
set.seed(123)

vari_1 = replicate(length(n), NA)
vari_2 = replicate(length(n), NA)

for (i in 1:length(n)){
  vari_1[i] = var(replicate(N_MC, T_1(rexp(n[i], rate = 1/theta))))
  vari_2[i] = var(replicate(N_MC, T_2(rexp(n[i], rate = 1/theta))))
}
```

Plots of the convergence paths:

```{r}
bias_plot_data = data.frame(sample_size=n, 
                           CRLB = theta^2/n,
                           Var_1 = vari_1,
                           Var_2 = vari_2)

ggplot(data = bias_plot_data, aes(x = sample_size)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = CRLB, color = "CRLB", linetype = "CRLB"), linewidth = 0.8) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = Var_1, color = "Var_1", linetype = "Var_1"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Var_2, color = "Var_2", linetype = "Var_2"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Legend", 
                     values = c("CRLB" = "deepskyblue4", 
                                "Var_1" = "darkorchid", 
                                "Var_2" = "brown1")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Legend", 
                        values = c("CRLB" = "solid", 
                                   "Var_1" = "dashed", 
                                   "Var_2" = "twodash"))
```

For a better comparison, start the plots at, say, n=10.

```{r}
ggplot(data = bias_plot_data[-c(1:7),], aes(x = sample_size)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = CRLB, color = "CRLB", linetype = "CRLB"), linewidth = 0.8) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = Var_1, color = "Var_1", linetype = "Var_1"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Var_2, color = "Var_2", linetype = "Var_2"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Legend", 
                     values = c("CRLB" = "deepskyblue4", 
                                "Var_1" = "darkorchid", 
                                "Var_2" = "brown1")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Legend", 
                        values = c("CRLB" = "solid", 
                                   "Var_1" = "dashed", 
                                   "Var_2" = "twodash"))
```

## f)

Construct a third estimator $T_3$ for $\theta$ which has (theoretically) a smaller variance than the other two and implement this as a function in R.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
T_3 = function(sample){6}
```

## g)

Compute the MSE of all three estimators as a function of sample size and compare those in one single figure. Add a meaningful legend and a title to your plot.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE, fig.align='center', fig.width = 10}
# Parameter
n = 3:100
set.seed(123)

# Vectors for later
mse_1 = replicate(length(n), NA)
mse_2 = replicate(length(n), NA)
mse_3 = replicate(length(n), NA)

for (i in 1:length(n)){
  mse_1[i] = MSE(replicate(N_MC, T_1(rexp(n[i], rate = 1/theta))), theta)
  mse_2[i] = MSE(replicate(N_MC, T_2(rexp(n[i], rate = 1/theta))), theta)
  mse_3[i] = MSE(replicate(N_MC, T_3(rexp(n[i], rate = 1/theta))), theta)
}

```

Plots:

```{r}
mse_plot_data = data.frame(sample_size=n,
                            MSE_1 = mse_1,
                            MSE_2 = mse_2,
                            MSE_3 = mse_3)

ggplot(data = mse_plot_data, aes(x = sample_size)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = MSE_1, color = "MSE_1", linetype = "MSE_1"), linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_line(aes(y = MSE_2, color = "MSE_2", linetype = "MSE_2"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = MSE_3, color = "MSE_3", linetype = "MSE_3"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Legend", 
                     values = c("MSE_1" = "deepskyblue4", 
                                "MSE_2" = "darkorchid", 
                                "MSE_3" = "brown1")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Legend", 
                        values = c("MSE_1" = "solid", 
                                   "MSE_2" = "dashed", 
                                   "MSE_3" = "twodash"))
```

Based on your previous results, argue why the MSE might be preferred to the variance as a loss function.

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE}
# Since T_1 and T_2 have higher variance than T_3, but lower bias, comparing only variances would be misleading.

# The MSE accounts for both bias and variance, and is therefore more appropriate for comparing estimator performance.

# Moreover, there is a well-known trade-off between bias and variance, which makes MSE a convex function with a unique minimum.
```

## Problem 2 (own work)

The random sample $\{X_i,\,i=1\ldots n\}$ is drawn from a Poisson distribution. Consider the following two estimators for $\lambda$:

$$
T_{mean} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\quad\text{and}\quad
T_{median} = \mathrm{median}(X_i)\,.
$$ For $\lambda = 4$ and $n = 1,2,\dots,100$, compute the MSE for the two estimators for different n and compare the MSE's in one single figure

```{r warning=FALSE, error=TRUE, fig.align='center', fig.width = 10}
# Parameter
n = 1:100
lambda = 4
set.seed(123)

# Vectors for later
mse_mean = replicate(length(n), NA)
mse_median = replicate(length(n), NA)

for (i in n){
  mse_mean[i] = MSE(replicate(N_MC, mean(rpois(n[i],lambda))), lambda)
  mse_median[i] = MSE(replicate(N_MC, median(rpois(n[i],lambda))), lambda)
}
```

Plots:

```{r}
mse_plot_pois = data.frame(sample_size=n,
                            MSE_mean = mse_mean,
                            MSE_median = mse_median)

ggplot(data = mse_plot_pois, aes(x = sample_size)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = MSE_mean, color = "MSE_mean", linetype = "MSE_mean"), size = 0.8) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = MSE_median, color = "MSE_median", linetype = "MSE_median"), size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Legend", 
                     values = c("MSE_mean" = "deepskyblue4", 
                                "MSE_median" = "darkorchid")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Legend", 
                        values = c("MSE_mean" = "solid", 
                                   "MSE_median" = "dashed")) + 
  ggtitle("MSE comparison for Poisson distribution")+
  ylab("MSE")
```
